source: TSTD project (TA 7305-CAM), "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដំណាំពោត" (Corn Cultivation Technical Manual), Section 6: Recording production costs/income and economic analysis, May 2012
text:
The manual explains why farmers should keep records of production costs and income. A farmer who does not record what was spent on production inputs cannot really know whether -- or why -- a crop was profitable or not. If a farmer only remembers total costs roughly (for example, 'about this much was spent') without a written record, they cannot judge accurately whether the harvest income actually covered costs. Once a farmer clearly understands their own input costs and output value, they can use that experience to make better decisions in future seasons, including planning which inputs are worth the expense.

Record keeping should cover two types of cost: (1) direct/paid costs (ចំណាយផ្ទាល់) -- actual cash spent on inputs such as seed, fertilizer, pesticide, fuel for water pumping, and rented tools/equipment used specifically for that crop; and (2) indirect/imputed costs (ចំណាយប្រយោល) -- the value of the farmer's own labor, land, and other resources used in production that were not paid out in cash but should still be counted as a real economic cost at local market rates, so that the true profitability of the crop can be judged.

The manual provides blank record-keeping templates for farmers to fill in: an input/expense table (product name, dates started and finished, and rows for each input type -- e.g., labor, land rental, seed, chemical fertilizer, manure, irrigation water, pesticide for disease, pesticide for insects, fuel for water pump, insect traps -- each with unit, quantity, unit price, and total cost) and a matching income table (product name, unit, quantity, unit price, and total value). A further worksheet totals variable costs (labor, land preparation, seed, fertilizers, pesticides, fuel) as Total Variable Cost (TVC), fixed costs (land tax/rent, tools depreciation, storage, interest, other fixed costs) as Total Fixed Cost (TFC), sums them as Total Cost (TC = TVC + TFC), and then computes cost per kilogram (TC divided by total yield) and price per kilogram (total income divided by total yield) so farmers can compare their production cost against the market selling price.
